source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5027896 (accepted author manuscript): abstract, sections 1-6, Key points box, disclosures and funding statement read in full; reference list checked for refs 12, 17, 19, 25, 28, 30, 36-38, 45, 47, 52-59, 78-80. No tables or figures in the article.

claims.overstatement: 'Olanzapine and haloperidol were both effective' and 'haloperidol and quetiapine both effective' repeat the review's wording ('efficacious'), but both trials were head-to-head comparisons without a placebo arm, and this same review states that psychotic symptoms commonly remit within about a week of abstinence without medication. What the trials show is similar improvement under either drug; efficacy against no treatment is not shown. Suggest 'symptoms improved similarly with both drugs (no placebo arm)'. Also, the Cochrane review and the 2005 trial are titled 'amphetamine psychosis' (Thai sample), so 'methamphetamine psychosis' is a slight narrowing.
claims.note: Every element of the claim is in this source: no large RCTs; one trial (N=58) in the 2009 Cochrane review, olanzapine and haloperidol both improved symptoms, olanzapine better tolerated with fewer extrapyramidal symptoms; a later double-blind RCT (Verachai et al., ref 80) of haloperidol vs quetiapine with remission in most participants on either drug; otherwise case reports, laboratory blockade studies and CBT evidence from schizophrenia. No placebo-controlled trial is described.

anchors.locator: 5. Treatment > 5.1 Treatment for acute methamphetamine psychosis, para 1
anchors.extracted: No large randomized trials of drug treatment for acute methamphetamine psychosis, so no evidence-based guideline; practice draws on case reports (risperidone, olanzapine; refs 38, 74-76) and on laboratory studies in which antipsychotics blocked amphetamine-induced psychosis. The 2009 Cochrane review (ref 78) included one small RCT (N=58; Leelahanaj 2005, 4-week double-blind olanzapine vs haloperidol): both improved psychotic symptoms; olanzapine significantly better tolerated with fewer extrapyramidal symptoms. A later double-blind RCT (ref 80) of haloperidol vs quetiapine: both tolerable, remission in a significant majority on either drug.

Remission within about 1 week of abstinence is reported across several studies, so many cases may resolve without medication; possible harms of D2 blockade (anhedonia, relapse) and a preclinical haloperidol interaction are weighed against possible protective effects; little is known about antipsychotic safety and efficacy in children and adolescents; CBT for methamphetamine-induced psychosis has not been formally studied (evidence borrowed from schizophrenia).

claims.note: This review is the source for three of the claim's figures: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence (two studies by overlapping authors, Chen et al. 2003 and 2005, refs 12 and 47), and 'nearly 40%' diagnosed with schizophrenia within 6 years in a Thai sample of more than 1,000 people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis (ref 57, Kittirattanapaiboon et al. 2010, first hospitalization). It also supports 'most resolve' (recovery on average within one week in early studies) and recurrence (nearly 50% of those admitted in Japan's second epidemic had a previous episode). Not in this source: 10-28% beyond 6 months, the 5% (China) figure, the 38.8% at 5 years and the 19.1-30% register figures. The denominator for the 16%/17% is written as 'of MA users', which is ambiguous (presumably those with psychosis). The review calls 16-17% 'very similar' to the Thai figure, which they are not; it may mean similar to each other.

anchors.extracted: In the earliest observational and experimental studies recovery was on average within one week (refs 28, 30, 52, 53); in a sizable subset an initial methamphetamine-induced psychosis 'converts' over years into a primary psychotic disorder with symptoms for 6 months or longer without use (refs 54-56). Thai sample of more than 1,000 people with at least one methamphetamine-induced psychotic episode: nearly 40% diagnosed with schizophrenia within 6 years of the first episode (ref 57). Two smaller studies: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence (refs 12, 47), none of whom had prior psychosis or a family history of schizophrenia.

In Japan's second epidemic nearly 50% of people admitted for methamphetamine psychosis had had a previous episode, some readmitted more than 10 times (Sato, ref 59); triggers include resumed use, even small amounts after long abstinence, but also other substances (heavy alcohol), sleep deprivation and psychosocial stress without methamphetamine; latency to recurrence after renewed use can be under a week.

Remission within 1 week of abstinence reported across a number of studies; transient psychotic symptoms in up to 40% of users (ref 17) are not a diagnosable disorder; a 1-month cut-off defines substance-induced vs primary psychosis in DSM-5, which the authors say may not fit some longer Japanese cases.

key_findings.correction: Minor: the 1-5 days is attributed to ref 28 (hourly intravenous d-amphetamine in healthy volunteers); ref 29 reports psychotic symptoms within 36 hours with oral dosing in people with prior intravenous use. Refs 28-32 are dated 1970-1974 as the card says.

The review writes '16% and 17% of MA users continued to experience psychosis after 1 and 3 months of abstinence'; 'of methamphetamine users with psychosis' is the card's reading of an ambiguous denominator, not the review's wording. Also, the 'very similar rates' phrase may mean similar to each other rather than to the Thai figure (see reporting issue 1).
Ref 88 confirmed as Patel et al. 2005 (atypical antipsychotics in aggressive children and adolescents).

reporting_issues.note: The 'very similar rates' sentence follows the Thai figure, but it can also be read as the two smaller studies being similar to each other (16% and 17%); either way the issue about non-independence (refs 12 and 47 share first authors: Chen, Lin, Sham, Ball, Loh) and the family-history tension stand.
Ref 17 is Schuckit 2006 (Addiction supplement, comorbidity in general).
Ref 76 Leucht et al. (new vs conventional antipsychotics, schizophrenia); ref 88 Patel et al. 2005; ref 63 Wright 1993 (mania following sleep deprivation).
Within this paper: Thai figure 'nearly 40% within 6 years'; latency 1.7 years in smokers vs 4.4 in injectors (ref 49, Matsumoto et al.).

interpretation_gap.note: One addition: the treatment section and Key points call olanzapine, haloperidol and quetiapine 'efficacious' on the basis of two head-to-head trials without placebo arms, while the same section says most cases remit within a week of abstinence without medication; the trials can show comparable improvement, not efficacy against the natural course.

missed: For cl_meth_psychosis_treatment: 'both effective' (claim) and 'both efficacious' (card KF10) rest on active-comparator trials with no placebo arm; given the review's own statement that symptoms commonly remit within about a week of abstinence, the claim should say symptoms improved similarly on either drug.

The Cochrane review (ref 78) and the 2005 trial (ref 79) are titled 'amphetamine psychosis'; only the later trial (ref 80, Verachai et al.) is titled methamphetamine-induced psychosis. Minor indirectness for a methamphetamine claim.
Section 5.1 para 3 contains medication-administration advice for agitation; the encyclopedia should not carry it into any page text (METHODS: no dosing or administration guidance).

Section 3.3 lists recurrence triggers that do not involve methamphetamine (heavy alcohol use, sleep deprivation, psychosocial stress); the claim's 'recurrence with renewed use' is accurate but is not the only recurrence pathway this source describes.
